Proposition 5 rewrites three sections of the California Constitution
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends Article II, sections 15 and 17, and Article V, section 10. It changes no statute directly. Its edits are short:
Section 15(a) strikes the words "and, if appropriate, to elect a successor" from the description of a recall election, leaving an election "to determine whether to recall an officer."
Section 15(c) strikes the sentence that makes "the candidate who receives a plurality" the successor, and strikes the ban on the targeted officer being a candidate. In their place it provides that if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
Article V, section 10(b) is new. If the Governor is removed by recall, "the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term," unless the recall comes "before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor's term." In that case "a special election shall be called to replace the Governor," consolidated with the statewide primary; a candidate with a majority at the primary takes office, and otherwise "the top two vote-getters shall compete in a special election consolidated with the subsequent statewide general election."
Section 17 moves the job of running a governor's recall from the lieutenant governor, who would now be the successor, to the secretary of state, with the controller taking over if the governor and secretary of state are targeted at the same time.
The Attorney General's ballot label calls it a change for "statewide officers," but the text applies to every state officer subject to recall, and the LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) describes its effect on Senate and Assembly seats as well. Prop 5 does not change how a recall qualifies, how quickly the election is held, or how local recalls work.
California recall law today: 12% of the last vote, two questions, a plurality winner
The power to recall is in Article II (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2014.&article=II) of the Constitution: "Recall is the power of the electors to remove an elective officer." A recall of a statewide officer needs signatures equal to 12% of the last vote for the office, including 1% of the last vote in each of five counties; senators, Assembly members, Board of Equalization members and appellate and trial judges need 20%. Proponents have 160 days to gather them, and the "sufficiency of reason is not reviewable." Once signatures are certified, the election is held 60 to 80 days later, or within 180 days to coincide with a regular election. An officer who survives is reimbursed for recall expenses, and no new recall can begin for six months.
The successor rule sits in section 15(c), last amended by Proposition 183 in 1994: if the majority votes to recall, "the officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate." Elections Code section 11385 repeats it: the candidate "receiving the highest number of votes for the office shall be declared elected for the unexpired term."
Prop 5 would replace that with the rules California already uses when an office falls vacant for any other reason. The lieutenant governor becomes governor under Article V, section 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=V). For the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, controller, treasurer, attorney general, superintendent of public instruction and Board of Equalization, Article V, section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=V) has the governor nominate a replacement who takes office on confirmation by a majority of each house, or automatically if neither house acts within 90 days. For a legislative seat, Elections Code section 10703 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=10703) requires a special election "at least 126 days, but not more than 140 days" after the governor's proclamation, which must be issued within 14 days of the vacancy.
California has already made this change for local officials. Since January 1, 2023, under AB 2582 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2582), recalls of local officers have asked only whether to remove the officer; under Elections Code section 11382 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=11382) the office "shall be vacant until it is filled according to law," and the recalled officer may not be appointed to the vacancy. Prop 5 uses the same structure and much of the same wording for state offices, which only a constitutional amendment can reach.
California recall elections are keeping their signature thresholds and timelines under Proposition 5 while the replacement question gives way to succession, appointment and special elections, as the measure's text and the California Constitution show in October 2026. The governor's seat under Prop 5: The lieutenant governor, then possibly a special election
For a recalled governor, Prop 5 creates a two-track rule keyed to timing. Late in a term, the lieutenant governor serves out the remainder, and no election is held for the seat until the next regular gubernatorial election. Early in a term, before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election during the governor's first two years, the lieutenant governor takes over and a special election is held alongside the next statewide primary. A majority winner there serves the rest of the term; without one, the top two meet again on the November ballot. The LAO's summary: the lieutenant governor "serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election" in the first case and "for the rest of the term" in the second.
Because Prop 5 removes the constitutional bar on the recalled officer's candidacy, a governor recalled early in a term could appear in that special election. The same applies to a recalled legislator in the special election that would fill the seat. The only limit the text adds is on appointment: a recalled officer "shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office."
That provision is the one even the measure's author has not defended. Newman told the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board he could not explain why it is there: "I'm honestly not sure," he said (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php). "It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there." The Yes campaign's website (https://fixtherecall.com/) presents it as a feature, saying that today's process "locks the recalled official out of the race entirely" and that under Prop 5 "the seat goes to a special election where every candidate can run." That description fits legislative seats and an early-term governor recall; for a governor recalled late in a term and for other statewide offices, the text provides succession or appointment, not an election.
California recall history: 182 attempts, 11 elections, six removals since 1913
The Secretary of State counts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) 182 attempts to recall state officials since 1913, 57 of them against governors. Eleven qualified for the ballot: nine against legislators and two against governors. Six succeeded: Senators Marshall Black (1913) and Edwin Grant (1914), Assembly members Paul Horcher (1994) and Doris Allen (1995), Governor Gray Davis (2003) and Senator Josh Newman (2018). No state recall effort is in circulation now, according to the Secretary of State's current-efforts page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/current-recall-efforts).
The three most recent recalls show what the replacement question does. In 2003 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2003-special/sum.pdf), 55.4% voted to recall Davis, and Arnold Schwarzenegger won the replacement contest with 4,206,284 votes, 48.6% of the votes for a candidate and more than the 4,007,783 cast to keep Davis. In 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-primary/sov/15-state-senator-29th-district.pdf), 58.1% voted to recall Newman in the 29th Senate District, and Republican Ling Ling Chang won the seat with 50,215 votes, 33.8% of the replacement vote and 15,982 fewer than the 66,197 cast for Newman to stay. In 2021 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/11-sov-summary.pdf), 61.9% voted against recalling Governor Newsom; the leading replacement candidate, Larry Elder, received 3,563,867 votes, which would have made him governor with 27.8% of the votes cast on the recall question had the recall passed. That is the "about 28%" figure in the Yes argument.
California recall results are showing replacement winners at 46.8% and 31.8% of the recall vote in 2003 and 2018, and 27.8% for 2021's leading candidate, in Secretary of State data compiled in October 2026. California is one of seven states that choose a successor on the same ballot as the recall, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures' survey (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials) of the 19 states that allow recall of state officials. Five others hold a separate special election and eight fill the vacancy by appointment, with some states mixing methods by office. Other reform ideas have taken different routes: the state's Little Hoover Commission recommended (https://lhc.ca.gov/press-release-43/) in 2022 a "snap" election in which "the targeted official is placed on the ballot with all potential replacements," plus a statewide signature threshold of 10% of registered voters. Prop 5 adopts neither.
Prop 5's cost: Savings or costs "in the range of millions of dollars," depending on the recall
The LAO's fiscal estimate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm) is "unknown," because it depends on how often recalls happen and which offices they target. Removing the second question would save money on ballots and voter materials when no follow-up election is needed, which is the case for a governor recalled late in a term and for offices filled by appointment. A legislative recall would cost more if the follow-up special election "could not be consolidated with a scheduled election," at "millions of dollars per election." The LAO puts the net effect at "savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars," less than 0.1% of the General Fund.
For scale, the Department of Finance's July 1, 2021 letter (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/dof-allocation-costs-letter.pdf) estimated $243.6 million for counties and $32.4 million for the Secretary of State, $276 million in all, of which the Legislature appropriated $250.2 million; the same letter estimated $90.6 million if the recall had been consolidated with a regular election. Prop 5 does not change the cost of the recall election itself, only of what follows it.
Proposition 5's author and the vote in the Legislature
Newman, a Fullerton Democrat, introduced SCA 1 in January 2023. It passed the Senate 31–7 on February 1, 2024 and, after amendment, the Assembly 59–17 on August 30, 2024; the Senate concurred 32–8 the next day, and it was filed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) with the Secretary of State on September 10, 2024, directed to this November's ballot. Constitutional amendments need two-thirds of each house. The Chronicle's editorial board notes that Newman was recalled in 2018, won the seat back in 2020 and lost again in 2024. Of the 2018 recall, which his opponents tie to his vote to raise gas taxes, he told CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/): "I didn't do anything other than cast a tough vote."
Nobody is spending money on the measure. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-5-sca-1-newman-elections-recall-state-officers-res-ch-204-2024) for Prop 5 reports "No committees identified" on either side as of October 6, and no Prop 5 committee appears on the FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), which covers committees that have raised $1 million. The Yes campaign's website is paid for by Californians For a Prosperous Golden State, the committee listed with Newman as the ballot contact. No opposition contact is listed in the Voter Information Guide.
The arguments: Majority rule versus the voters' pick
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause and former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, says the two questions together create "a dangerous loophole": "An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast." It cites the 2021 recall's cost as "more than $200 million" and says Prop 5 would stop recalls being used "to 'redo' an election as a political or partisan scheme." The Department of Finance's figures above support the cost claim; the 28% figure matches the Statement of Vote.
The No argument, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson, says Prop 5 "will take away your voice" because "politicians themselves—not voters—would choose who fills the vacancy" in many cases, and other seats "would sit vacant until another costly election." It objects that "that failed politician you just ran out the door… they'd be allowed to run in that next election," and its rebuttal says the author wants to change the rules after being recalled "when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises." Carl DeMaio, the Prop 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/) proponent, told CalMatters voters could be "without a representative for months, if not longer." Polling and endorsements on Proposition 5
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, reading the ballot title "Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers," found 35% yes, 59% no and 5% undecided, the weakest position of any measure on the ballot. Opposition crossed party lines: Democrats 40% yes to 54% no, Republicans 34% to 64%, independents 28% to 65%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 1% named Prop 5. No other independent poll has published a Prop 5 result.
The parties split along legislative lines: the California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 5 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom, the target of the 2021 recall, plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The editorial boards are divided. McClatchy's California board, writing for the Sacramento Bee and four other papers, endorsed (https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/proposition-5-could-change-california-173000601.html) it on September 18 because it "respects the democratic norm of majority rule." The San Francisco Chronicle's board recommended a no vote on October 8: it agreed "the second question is problematic" but called the provision letting recalled officials run again "a completely unnecessary provision" and "reason enough for voters to reject this measure."
Proposition 5 after November 3: A one-question recall from mid-December or the 1994 rule
If Prop 5 passes, it takes effect under Article XVIII, section 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII) on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11. Any state recall after that would ask a single question, and the Elections Code sections that still describe a successor contest, such as section 11385, would sit under an amended Constitution that no longer provides for one. If it fails, state recalls keep the two-question ballot and plurality winner that section 15 has required since 1994, while local recalls continue under the one-question rule in place since 2023. Either way, the signature thresholds that decide how often Californians face a recall are not on this ballot.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

This ballot measure blocks voters from instantly replacing politicians, leaving Sacramento insiders untouchable

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 20, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 21, 2026 at 11:17 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.
Related Articles
Endorsement: Break the 49ers’ grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)
Endorsement: These three City Council candidates are San Jose’s best choices (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

Right now, a recall election asks Californians two questions at once.
The second one is the problem: it hands the seat to whoever finishes first in a crowded field, sometimes with a sliver of the vote, and it locks the recalled official out of the race entirely.
The Solution
Proposition 5 puts the decision back where it belongs.
Recall an official, and the seat goes to a special election where every candidate can run and voters choose a replacement outright. This isn’t about protecting any party or any officeholder. It’s about making sure the person who ends up in the seat actually won it.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Is a hissy fit worth $200 million (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-02-03/california-recall-election-cost-200-million-dollars)?
That was the tab in 2021, when California held a recall election (https://www.latimes.com/topic/newsom-recall) less than a year before Gov. Gavin Newsom was set to face voters.
There was angst —the COVID-19 pandemic was raging (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-19/l-a-county-covid-19-deaths-top-25000-as-delta-spreads). There was anger — the lifesaving restrictions (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-12-13/california-orders-statewide-mask-order-starting-wednesday) imposed by Washington and Sacramento made daily living a chore (https://www.latimes.com/science/coronavirus-one-year-later) and drove many small businesses to the brink. Others went clear over the edge (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2020-10-29/coronavirus-pandemic-small-business-southern-california).
There was also no small amount of political opportunism at play.
The recall gave Newsom’s critics, mainly on the right, a chance to try to chase the Democrat from an office (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-27/recall-backers-have-california-ideas-beyond-newsom-defeat) that Republicans, under normal circumstances, stood little chance of winning.
Advertisement
In the end, the recall effort amounted to scarcely more than a partisan tantrum. The result — 61.9% voting no, 38.1% voting yes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-14/recall-election-california-newsom-results) — matched the outcome of the 2018 gubernatorial race (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-california-governor-race-20181106-story.html) down to the decimal. All that money and effort wasted on an election in which voters said pretty much, yep, we meant what we said. Not too long after, they gave Newsom a second term (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-08/2022-california-election-governor-newsom-dahle-results).
The plebiscite, and its pointlessness (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-15/newsom-california-recall-election-costly-lessons), underscored the many flaws inherent in California’s recall system. In November, voters will get a chance to remedy at least one of them, eliminating the chance a candidate could take office with just marginal support from voters.

One choice, not two
Currently, a recall election is conducted in two parts. Voters are asked whether a lawmaker should be removed and, if so, who their replacement should be. If the incumbent is ousted, whoever gets the most votes takes their place, even if they fall well shy of attaining majority support. (Which is not out of the question in a large multi-candidate field; in 2003, 135 people were on the ballot (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-27-me-recallqa27-story.html), vying to replace Gov. Gray Davis (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html).)
Among its provisions, Proposition 5 would amend the state Constitution so that voters would be asked a simple yes-or-no question: Do you wish to recall the incumbent? If so, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the rest of the ousted executive’s term — unless the recall occurred during the first two years a governor was in office and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election.
In that case, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor’s term. If no candidate received a majority, the top-two finishers would face each other in a November runoff, with the winner taking over as governor.
Still there?
Proposition 5 has two benefits. It would save taxpayer dollars by consolidating elections and it would enhance the legitimacy and political standing of a replacement governor by ensuring he or she assumed office with at least 50% support.
But there’s still more to be done (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-23/california-recall-reform-efforts-stall).
Ending political promiscuity
California makes it way too easy to qualify a gubernatorial recall measure.
Of the 19 states that allow their governor to be booted, California is by far the most permissive. Forcing an election requires signatures reflecting just 12% of the ballots cast in the prior gubernatorial contest. In Newsom’s case, proponents needed just under 1.5 million signatures in a state with more than 22 million voters and nearly 40 million residents.
Not exactly a thundering roar.
The threshold should be higher and the reasons for kicking a governor out of office should be more serious, such as corruption, official malfeasance or conviction for a serious crime. Not just because a governor is a member of the opposite party (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-03-01/newsom-recall-sore-losers-are-undermining-democracy), orpeople on the losing end (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-04-13/newsom-recall-revolt-red-vs-blue-california) of an election are unhappy with the result.

California Must Address Weakness in the State’s Recall System, Urges Little Hoover Commission
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
February 8, 2022
For Additional Information Contact:
Ethan Rarick, Executive Director (510) 205-8042
California should adjust the signature requirement for recalling statewide office-holders and revise the recall election process to put the incumbent on the ballot against all challengers, urges the state’s independent government watchdog in its new report.
In Reforming the Recall (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall) the Little Hoover Commission evaluates the state’s recall process, examines the advantages and drawbacks of different recall reforms, and offers recommendations to strengthen the recall system.
“The recall is a popular tool of direct democracy that has been a significant component of the state’s electoral system for over a century,” says Commission Chair Pedro Nava. “We must keep the recall, but California must address fundamental flaws within current recall procedures that leave the system vulnerable to abuse and pave the way for a potentially undemocratic outcome.”
In its report, the Commission recommends that California change the signature requirement for recalling statewide office-holders from 12 percent of the vote in the last election for the office to 10 percent of registered voters. This adjustment will reduce fluctuations in the signature threshold as a result of differences in voter turnout between elections, providing greater consistency in the recall process. It will also increase the number of signatures required to initiate a recall election, discouraging overuse of the recall while keeping it accessible as a tool of electoral accountability.
The Commission further recommends that the state replace the existing two-part recall ballot with a “snap” special recall election. Under this system, the targeted official is placed on the ballot with all potential replacements.
“Under the current recall system a replacement candidate can win office even if they received fewer votes than the recalled incumbent,” says Chair Nava. “The core reason that the Commission supports the use of snap elections for recalls is that it would protect the democratic principle that the person who receives the most votes should win.”
The report follows a lengthy study process that included three public hearings at which Commissioners heard testimony from current and former elected officials such as Secretary of State Shirley Weber and former Secretary of State Bill Jones. The Commission also took testimony from a wide array of scholars and other experts, and received comment from more than 150 members of the public.
The Commission also outlines procedural reforms, which would give elections officials more time to administer elections and provide greater clarity around the recall process.
Several of the Commission’s recommendations—including those outlined above—must be approved by voters. The Commission urges the Legislature to propose recall reforms separately, to give voters the opportunity to pick which changes they think should be adopted.
“The Commission’s recommendations will bolster California’s recall system by helping the state better balance voters’ right to recall officials with protection for electoral integrity and democratic principles,” says Chair Nava.
About the Little Hoover Commission
The Little Hoover Commission is America’s only permanent, independent citizens commission working to improve state government. A nonpartisan oversight agency created in 1962, the Commission includes 13 Commissioners appointed by the Governor and legislative leaders. The Commission’s mission is to investigate state operations and promote efficiency, economy, and improved service.

Ideas expressed in the piece
The column contends that California’s gubernatorial recall process has become a costly outlet for partisan grievance, pointing to the 2021 effort against Gov. Gavin Newsom as an expensive, largely redundant re-litigation of the 2018 election rather than a meaningful exercise in accountability [5] (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article253864413.html) . It suggests that such recalls siphon public money and attention from governance while merely confirming outcomes voters had already endorsed [5] (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article253864413.html) .
The article argues that the core structural flaw in California’s recall rules is the two-question ballot, which allows voters to remove an incumbent by majority vote while simultaneously electing a replacement who may win with only a small plurality [2] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2022-02-13/editorial-californias-recall-rules-could-let-a-loser-win-its-time-to-change-that) [6] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2024-03-19/editorial-newsom-recall-still-not-fixed-undemocratic-rules) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-16/skelton-recall-constitutionality-newsom-california-governor) . It notes that in a crowded field this can produce a scenario where a governor receives far more votes than the successor yet still loses office, a result critics in other commentaries have labeled undemocratic and potentially unconstitutional [2] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2022-02-13/editorial-californias-recall-rules-could-let-a-loser-win-its-time-to-change-that) [6] (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2024-03-19/editorial-newsom-recall-still-not-fixed-undemocratic-rules) [11] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-16/skelton-recall-constitutionality-newsom-california-governor) .
Building on that critique, the piece supports Proposition 5, a legislatively referred constitutional amendment on the November 2026 ballot that would eliminate the simultaneous successor election and ask a single yes-or-no question about recalling the incumbent [4] (https://fullertonobserver.com/2026/08/15/california-proposition-5-2026-eliminating-the-successor-election-in-state-officer-recalls/) [7] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) [12] (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-5/) . It explains that, under the measure, a recalled governor’s seat would be filled either by the lieutenant governor for the remainder of the term or, when the recall occurs early in a term, by a special election in which the winner must secure a majority, with a runoff if necessary, thereby ensuring the replacement takes office with broader voter support [4] (https://fullertonobserver.com/2026/08/15/california-proposition-5-2026-eliminating-the-successor-election-in-state-officer-recalls/) [7] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) [12] (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-5/) .
The column further maintains that California’s signature threshold for initiating a gubernatorial recall—12% of votes cast in the previous governor’s race, roughly 1.5 million signatures in Newsom’s case—makes it too easy for a relatively small, motivated minority to force a statewide election [9] (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/prior-elections/statewide-election-results/2021-ca-gov-recall/newsom-recall-faqs) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) . It argues that the bar should be higher and that grounds for recall should be limited to serious misconduct such as corruption or criminal conviction, echoing concerns in oversight reports that the current open-ended standard invites overuse and abuse of the process [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) [10] (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250011419.html) .
In addition, the piece suggests that the recall has drifted from its Progressive-era good-government roots into a tool for “bad actors” who can target officials they simply dislike and potentially install successors lacking majority support [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . It cites reform recommendations from the Little Hoover Commission, which has urged changes such as raising the signature requirement and restricting recall timing, as evidence that independent watchdogs also see the existing framework as vulnerable to manipulation and in need of modernization [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
Different views on the topic
A law review article argues that California’s recall system is not overpowered and, in fact, functions much as its Progressive-era designers intended: as a difficult but potent “voter weapon” to menace and remove public officials when necessary [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . It notes that from 1911 to 2021, 179 recall petitions were filed against state officials, but only 11 qualified for the ballot and just six succeeded, a record the piece uses to contend that recalls are already rare and that fears of rampant abuse are overstated [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .
While sharing concerns about undemocratic outcomes, some reform advocates favor a different structural fix than Proposition 5, proposing a “snap” special recall election in which the incumbent appears on the ballot alongside all challengers rather than leaving the office temporarily vacant [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) . The Little Hoover Commission, for example, recommends replacing the two-part ballot with such a system and adjusting the signature requirement to 10% of registered voters, arguing that this approach both raises the bar for launching a recall and ensures that any successor must defeat the incumbent directly in a single election [1] (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/FactSheet266.pdf) [8] (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) .
The law review piece also emphasizes the historical role of the recall as a central Progressive innovation that gives voters a direct tool to check officials between regular election cycles, and it warns that sweeping restrictions on who can initiate recalls or on permissible reasons could blunt that instrument of accountability [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) . By stressing that recall attempts are frequently filed but rarely successful, the article suggests that the existing hurdles already filter out frivolous efforts and that tightening the rules further could unduly insulate incumbents from public pressure [3] (https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2938&context=lawreview) .

Reforming the Recall
Report #266, February 2022
OVERVIEW
California should adjust the signature requirement for recalling statewide office-holders and revise the recall election process to put the incumbent on the ballot against all challengers, urges the state’s independent government watchdog in its new report.
In Reforming the Recall, (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf)the Little Hoover Commission evaluates the state’s recall process, examines the advantages and drawbacks of different recall reforms, and offers recommendations to strengthen the recall system.
“The recall is a popular tool of direct democracy that has been a significant component of the state’s electoral system for over a century,” says Commission Chair Pedro Nava. “We must keep the recall, but California must address fundamental flaws within current recall procedures that leave the system vulnerable to abuse and pave the way for a potentially undemocratic outcome.”
In its report, the Commission recommends that California change the signature requirement for recalling statewide office-holders from 12 percent of the vote in the last election for the office to 10 percent of registered voters. This adjustment will reduce fluctuations in the signature threshold as a result of differences in voter turnout between elections, providing greater consistency in the recall process. It will also increase the number of signatures required to initiate a recall election, discouraging overuse of the recall while keeping it accessible as a tool of electoral accountability.
The Commission further recommends that the state replace the existing two-part recall ballot with a “snap” special recall election. Under this system, the targeted official is placed on the ballot with all potential replacements.
“Under the current recall system a replacement candidate can win office even if they received fewer votes than the recalled incumbent,” says Chair Nava. “The core reason that the Commission supports the use of snap elections for recalls is that it would protect the democratic principle that the person who receives the most votes should win.”
The report follows a lengthy study process that included three public hearings at which Commissioners heard testimony from current and former elected officials such as Secretary of State Shirley Weber and former Secretary of State Bill Jones. The Commission also took testimony from a wide array of scholars and other experts, and received comment from more than 150 members of the public.
The Commission also outlines procedural reforms, which would give elections officials more time to administer elections and provide greater clarity around the recall process.
Several of the Commission’s recommendations—including those outlined above—must be approved by voters. The Commission urges the Legislature to propose recall reforms separately, to give voters the opportunity to pick which changes they think should be adopted.
“The Commission’s recommendations will bolster California’s recall system by helping the state better balance voters’ right to recall officials with protection for electoral integrity and democratic principles,” says Chair Nava.
Written testimony from hearing witnesses can be found in the corresponding event agenda.

Reforming the Recall
Report #266 | February 2022
Milton Marks Commission on California State
Government Organization and Economy
www.lhc.ca.gov
Dedicated to Promoting Economy
and Efficiency in California State
Government
The Little Hoover Commission, formally known as the Milton
Marks “Little Hoover” Commission on California State Government
Organization and Economy, is an independent state oversight agency.
By statute, the Commission is a bipartisan board composed of
five public members appointed by the governor, four public
members appointed by the Legislature, two senators and two
assemblymembers.
In creating the Commission in 1962, the Legislature declared its
purpose:
...to secure assistance for the Governor and itself in
promoting economy, efficiency and improved services in the
transaction of the public business in the various departments,
agencies and instrumentalities of the executive branch of
the state government, and in making the operation of all
state departments, agencies and instrumentalities, and
all expenditures of public funds, more directly responsive
to the wishes of the people as expressed by their elected
representatives...
The Commission fulfills this charge by listening to the public,
consulting with the experts and conferring with the wise. In the
course of its investigations, the Commission typically empanels
advisory committees, conducts public hearings and visits government
operations in action.
Its conclusions are submitted to the Governor and the Legislature
for their consideration. Recommendations often take the form of
legislation, which the Commission supports through the legislative
process.
Contacting the Commission

Letter from the Chair
February 8, 2022
The Honorable Gavin Newsom
Governor of California
The Honorable Toni Atkins The Honorable Scott Wilk
